title: Budget bores have more fun? Financial clarity rivals income for wellbeing benefits, new research suggests | Klarna International
body_markdown:
**New York, October 23, 2026** — It’s not just the size of our income that counts. Financial clarity may be just as important for wellbeing as income, and could even help us look forward to a vacation more, according to new research by two leading behavioral scientists.


Published today as


[The Clarity Effect](https://www.klarna.com/uk/the-clarity-effect?utm_source=press-release&utm_medium=press&utm_campaign=the-clarity-effect)


, the research studied this less-explored aspect of consumer finance through randomized experiments that kept money the same and changed only how clearly people could see it. Carried out for Klarna, the everyday finance network, in collaboration with mental wellbeing app Headspace, the research was done by Professor Paul Dolan of the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE).


The Clarity Effect found a predictable income was more closely linked to life satisfaction than how much someone earned. Similarly, being able to cover an unexpected bill was about twice as strongly linked to life satisfaction as income.


Even though income and expenditure was unchanged in two experimental groups, people given greater financial clarity in the experiments looked forward to plans more, felt more in control and made fewer budgeting mistakes. For some, it even qualitatively boosted creativity.


The findings challenge common assumptions like money buying happiness and budgeting being tedious, suggesting instead that consumers can feel better about their finances and free up headspace to think more enjoyable thoughts without increasing their income.


**Professor Dolan said:** “We tend to assume that people who keep track of their money are missing out on fun. Our research suggests the opposite: when you’re on top of your finances, your mind is free to wander to fun places, including future experiences. Knowing where you stand isn’t boring, it’s what helps you free up headspace and boost wellbeing.” Dolan has been supported in his research by Professor Micael Dalen of the Stockholm School of Economics - together the pair are known as The Happy Profs for their groundbreaking work in the field.


Consumer research commissioned by Klarna shows how much money follows Americans on vacation. Six in ten (60%) say thoughts about money distract them from enjoying a trip and 65% regularly tally up what they’ve spent while away. Yet 71% agree that being clear about their finances before they go means they think about money less while they’re away.


In the headline experiment, the Holiday Test, UK participants given a budgeting tool when planning a trip looked forward to it more and pictured it more vividly. When asked to imagine the vacation afterward, those without the tool were more likely to think of money (11% vs 3%).


**Magnus Lindholm, Head of Consumer Marketing at Klarna said:** “Financial tools should give people the clarity and confidence to make informed decisions, without money becoming a constant distraction. Like a good football referee, they should work in the background, stepping in when needed to keep things running smoothly.”


Clarity was closely linked with certainty. The consumer research found 76% of Americans would rather know the full cost of something upfront, even if it’s higher than wanted. In experiments, people waiting for a car repair bill felt about 15% more in control when told the exact price than when told it would fall within a range, even though the expected cost was the same.


The opportunity is significant: money takes up a lot of our headspace, and clarity can help win some of it back. Money is effectively tied with family as the most frequent everyday thought for Americans (71% vs 72% think about it daily), ahead of physical health (65%) and career (58%), and 31% think about it four or more times a day, according to Klarna’s consumer research.


**Dr Jenna Glover, Chief Clinical Officer at Headspace, said:** “People often assume that earning more reduces stress, but psychologically what calms us is a sense of control. Financial clarity eases the mental load, giving you both the confidence you can cover the unexpected and the headspace to enjoy life to the fullest”.


Klarna partnered with Headspace to share practical tips for reducing the mental load of money, including:


-


**Keep everything in one place:** People experienced higher financial clarity when their income and bills were organised in a single view


-


**Track a running total:** Keeping a budget reduced the risk of overspending and boosted positive feelings of anticipation


-


**Get costs confirmed early:** Knowing the exact amount of a bill made people feel more in control. Ask for fixed quotes and confirm amounts upfront where possible


-


**Know where you stand, but don’t over-check:** Frequently checking a balance was linked to more worry, not more happiness


**Notes to Editors**


-


*The full Clarity Effect report is available*[HERE](https://www.klarna.com/uk/the-clarity-effect?utm_source=press-release&utm_medium=press&utm_campaign=the-clarity-effect)


*. Experiments ran July through September 2026 with more than 1,500 UK adults. Online participants were recruited through Sago*


-


*Consumer research was commissioned by Klarna among nationally representative samples of 2,000 adults each in the U.S. and UK, and 1,000 adults each in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. Fieldwork took place between 16th and 23rd September 2026. The research was conducted via 3Gem’s in-house, double opt-in panel of pre-recruited respondents, whose identities have been twice verified. 3Gem adheres to MRS standards and is a member of ESOMAR, BPC and GPQ*

**About the Professors**
Paul Dolan and Micael Dalen are behavioral science experts specializing in happiness, wellbeing, and decision-making.


*The Clarity Effect* report was commissioned by Klarna to explore the psychological relationship between money and everyday headspace.
